t: Section 563 of the Act approved March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 1279), as amended (sec. 1–506, D.C. Code, 1961 ed.), is amended to read as follows: “Each notary’ public shall file his signature and deposit an impression of his official seal with the Commissioners of the District of Columbia or their designated agent, and the Commissioners or their designated agent may certify to the authenticity of the signature and official seal of the notary public.”

fable.w: The tempting reading is that notaries (outside parties) interacting with the D.C. Commissioners amounts to participation. But this is only an administrative filing requirement (signature and seal) plus an authority to certify authenticity. No outside party is consulted on, comments on, or may challenge any government decision, and there is no hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.
fable.s: shall file his signature and deposit an impression of his official seal with the Commissioners of the District of Columbia or their designated agent

qwen_block.w: This section describes a procedural requirement for notaries public to file documents with government officials (the Commissioners of the District of Columbia). It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by outside parties in a federal decision-making process. The interaction is a one-way filing for record-keeping purposes, not a participatory mechanism like a hearing, comment period, or advisory board.
qwen_block.s: Each notary’ public shall file his signature and deposit an impression of his official seal with the Commissioners of the District of Columbia or their designated agent, and the Commissioners or their designated agent may certify to the authenticity of the signature and official seal of the notary public.

opus.w: This provision only requires notaries to file their signatures and seal impressions so the Commissioners can certify that they are authentic. Someone outside the government (the notary) does deal with an official body, which could look like participation. But this is a ministerial filing, much like a registration or license record. It does not consult or coordinate with outsiders before any policy decision, and it creates no hearing, comment period, advisory body or right to sue.
opus.s: Each notary’ public shall file his signature and deposit an impression of his official seal with the Commissioners of the District of Columbia or their designated agent

qwen_chat.w: This section describes an administrative filing requirement for notaries public to register their signatures and seals with the District of Columbia Commissioners. This is a licensing or registration process, not a consultation, public hearing, or advisory committee process involving outside parties in federal decision-making. The definition excludes applications for benefits or licenses, and this interaction does not involve the federal government consulting with outsiders before making a policy decision.
qwen_chat.s: Each notary’ public shall file his signature and deposit an impression of his official seal with the Commissioners of the District of Columbia or their designated agent, and the Commissioners or their designated agent may certify to the authenticity of the signature and official seal of the notary public.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the notary public is an "outside party" (a private citizen) interacting with the government (the Commissioners), and thus this constitutes participation. However, the definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants" and generally treats administrative filings or licensing requirements as non-participatory. The notary is not consulting on a policy decision, nor is there a public hearing or advisory board involved. The interaction is a unilateral administrative filing required for professional registration, not a collaborative decision-making process.
